title: Oscar Wilde, The Happy Prince recast
author: Vellum
note: A gold-leaf statue above the harbour gives itself away; a late swallow stays; the city calls the bare pedestal an improvement. After Wilde, The Happy Prince, 1888.

scenes.title: Above the harbour
scenes.reentry: High above Victoria Harbour the Happy Prince stood in gold leaf, sapphire eyes, a ruby at his sword hilt—commissioned by a committee that loved skyline photographs and disliked complaints from the street.

breaths.text: High above Victoria Harbour the Happy Prince stood in gold leaf, sapphire eyes, a ruby at his sword hilt—commissioned by a committee that loved skyline photographs and disliked complaints from the street.
Tour buses paused.
Couples posed.
A drone hummed like a bored insect.
By day he shone for tourists who framed him between ferry wakes and tower glass.

By night he saw what the photographs cropped: a child sewing until her fingers bled in a subdivided flat in Sham Shui Po; an old man in a cardboard lee near the Star Ferry, counting coins that would not become a room; a boy too feverish for school and too poor for the clinic’s patience; a young man staring at black water as if water were an exit with better manners than the city.
A swallow, late for migration south, rested between the prince’s feet out of exhaustion and bad timing.
Wind off the harbour smelled of salt, diesel, and someone’s late dinner.
Neon stuttered across the prince’s gold.
“Stay one night,” the prince said, though statues are not supposed to speak and cities punish sincerity.
“Take the ruby to the sewing girl.
I can see her lamp from here—one square of yellow in a building that should not still be standing.
I cannot move.
You can.”
The swallow, who had planned on warmer air and easier gossip among birds along some kinder coast, obeyed because the prince’s voice held a sadness that was not decorative.
She flew through canyons of glass, past laundry poles and air-conditioners dripping onto alleys, and laid the ruby beside a needle that never rested.

Night after night the command continued—sapphire for the feverish child, sapphire for the man who sold matches with shaking hands outside a 7-Eleven that never closed—then the gold leaf stripped in soft sheets until the prince stood dull and sincere in the typhoon wind, lead showing through like honesty.
Rain slicked him.
The swallow grew cold and did not leave.
Love, in this city as in others, is often a refusal to catch the last flight.
Below them Hong Kong went on making money and light.
The Mid-Levels escalator climbed its patient machine prayer.
Boardrooms practiced the grammar of growth.
A charity gala raised funds under chandeliers while a singer covered a ballad about resilience; the prince, now bare, watched the same hungers the gala would later call “issues” on a slide deck.
When morning officials found the statue stripped, they called it an eyesore and a liability, possibly vandalism, possibly a bad metaphor.
A councillor with a fondness for metrics and ribbon-cuttings ordered it pulled down before the press could invent a narrative about civic shame.
Cranes arrived with the cheerfulness of progress.
Tourists photographed the demolition as content for strangers.
In the foundry the broken prince melted beside common scrap; his leaden heart lagged in the heat, stubborn as a conscience.
“How ugly he became without the gold,” someone said, meaning: how useless without shine, how inconvenient without spectacle.

They found the swallow dead at the base, feathers pasted with harbour grit, and swept it into a bag with ticket stubs, a crushed can, and a flyer for a property launch promising harbour views to people who already owned the horizon.
Far above administrative weather—above the Peak, above the apps that rate restaurants and ignore hunger—something older than committees received the bird and the heart that would not melt cleanly.
On the emptied pedestal a newer sculpture arrived within a month: abstract, sponsored by a bank, impossible to pity, excellent for drone footage and year-end reports.
The city, which understands spectacle the way a mirror understands faces, called it an improvement.
The harbour kept its glamour.
The poor kept their nights.
And somewhere a child slept warmer for one week because a swallow had once believed a prince who had finally learned what his gold was for.
